title: Simulation & Inference

N = 1000


Code
final_year    <- 80
n_individuals <- 1000

outcome_matrix <- matrix(NA, 
                         nrow = n_individuals,
                         ncol = final_year)

FOI                 <- 0.05
prob_inf            <- rep(1 - exp(-FOI), n_individuals)
previously_infected <- rep(0, n_individuals)

set.seed(1534)

for(year_of_age in 1:final_year)
{
  prob_inf <- ifelse(previously_infected, 0, prob_inf)
  
  outcomes <- rbern(n = n_individuals, prob = prob_inf)
  
  outcome_matrix[, year_of_age] <- outcomes
  
  previously_infected <- previously_infected | outcomes
}

outcome_df <- data.frame(
  individual   = rep(seq_len(n_individuals), each = final_year),
  age          = rep(seq_len(final_year), times = n_individuals),
  was_infected = as.vector(t(outcome_matrix)))




Code
serostatus_df <- outcome_df |> 
  group_by(individual) |> 
  mutate(serostatus = cumsum(was_infected)) |> 
  ungroup()

set.seed(1541)

birth_df <- data.frame(individual = 1:n_individuals, 
                       birth_year = sample(1947:2026,
                                           size = n_individuals,
                                           replace = TRUE))

serostatus_by_year_df <- serostatus_df |> 
  left_join(birth_df, by = "individual") |> 
  mutate(year_sample = birth_year + age - 1)

sample_2026_df <- serostatus_by_year_df |> filter(year_sample == 2026)




Code
ggplot(sample_2026_df, aes(age)) +
  geom_dots(aes(colour = as.factor(serostatus),
                fill   = as.factor(serostatus),
                group  = NA,
                order  = serostatus),
            binwidth = 1, layout = "bin",
            overflow = "compress") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "#96595A")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "#96595A")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, final_year + 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Age") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text    = element_text(size = 12),
        axis.title   = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.line    = element_line(colour = "grey65"),
        axis.line.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")

title: Simulation & Inference
text:
Log-likelihood function


Code
log_likelihood_function <- function(FOI)
{
  if(FOI < 0) return -Inf
  
  y_a     <- seropositive_proportion_by_age_df$n_seropositive
  
  n_a     <- seropositive_proportion_by_age_df$n_individuals
  
  ages    <- seropositive_proportion_by_age_df$age
  
  prob_a  <-  1 - exp(-FOI * ages) # Serocatalytic model
  
  log_likelihood_values <- dbinom(x    = y_a,
                                  size = n_a,
                                  prob = prob_a,
                                  log  = TRUE)
  
  -sum(log_likelihood_values)
}




Code
optim_output <- optim(par = c(FOI = 0.01),
                      fn =  log_likelihood_function)

title: Session 2: Serocatalytic Models
text:
In this practical, we are going to be fitting serocatalytic models to cross-sectional serological data using the R package Rsero. In Rsero the models are fitted to data using Markov Chain Monte Carlo implemented through Stan, a probabalistic programming language.



The aims of this practical are to:

Estimate the force of infection by fitting serocatalytic models to serological datasets using MCMC
Compare different models with different assumptions about historical transmission and decide which one fits the data best
Reconstruct past circulation of pathogens in the population




First, we will load in the R packages that we need


Code
library(Rsero)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr) # we use this to arrange and save multiple plots together


and download the simulated cross-sectional serology datasets used in this practical:

Simulated dataset 1
Simulated dataset 2

Each file contains a simulated dataset for 1000 participants, with sampling in 2024. The dataset has columns participant_id, age, and serostatus for 1,000 participants. Note when loading this in on the R instance you will want to use this file path: read.csv("./simulated-data1.csv.


Code
data_1 <- read.csv("../data/simulated-data1.csv")
data_2 <- read.csv("../data/simulated-data2.csv")





Let’s start with the first simulation dataset (data_1). We’ll group the data into 10 year age bins and then visualise seroprevalence by age.


Code
agg_data_1 <- data_1 |> 
  mutate(age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(seq(0, 70, by = 10), Inf),
      labels = c(
        "0-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30-39",
        "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70+"),
      right = FALSE)) |> 
  group_by(age_group)  |> 
  summarise(n = n(),
            seropositive = sum(serostatus),
            seroprevalence = mean(serostatus),
            seroprevalence = seropositive / n,
            ci_lower = binom.test(seropositive, n)$conf.int[1],
            ci_upper = binom.test(seropositive, n)$conf.int[2], .groups = "drop")

ggplot(agg_data_1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = age_group, y = seroprevalence)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = age_group, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "Seroprevalence")












Next, we will prepare the data for use with RSero. RSero needs data to be in SeroData format, which needs the participants’ age at the time of sampling (age_at_sampling) and serostatus (Y).


Code
sero_data1 <- SeroData(age_at_sampling = data_1$age, Y = data_1$serostatus, sampling_year = 2024)
sero_data2 <- SeroData(age_at_sampling = data_2$age, Y = data_2$serostatus, sampling_year = 2024)


We will now define some serocatalytic models to test.
In RSero you can specify several different models of force-of-infection over time. We will look at the following.
- Constant. This is the simplest (classic) serocatalytic model which assumes a constant force of infection over time. This works well for endemic pathogens that circulate continuously in the population and are fully immunising. - Piecewise-constant. This is an extension of the classic model where we assume there have been several periods of constant force of infection. This would work well (for example) if an intervention had recently been introduced which lowered the force of infection at a particular point in time. - Outbreak. This model describes pathogen with epidemic dynamics where there have been K epidemics in the past. The model will estimate the force of infection and the timing of K previous outbreaks, assuming that FOI can be described by K Gaussian-shaped curves.


Code
constant_model <- FOImodel(type = "constant")
piecewise_model <- FOImodel(type = "piecewise", K = 2) # assuming there have been 2 phases with distinct force of infection
outbreak_model <- FOImodel(type = "outbreak", K = 1) # assuming there has been 1 outbreak in the past


Now let’s fit each model - this may take a few minutes.
You should see output from Stan on your console showing you how the sampling is progressing for each model and potentially giving you some warnings about the fit.


Code
constant_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = constant_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)
piecewise_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = piecewise_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)
outbreak_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = outbreak_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)





We now have three different model fits, with very different underlying assumptions about historical transmission. First let’s compare how well each of them fit the data visually. We can do this using the RSero function seroprevalence.fit().


Code
constant_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(constant_fit_1)
piecewise_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(piecewise_fit_1)
outbreak_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(outbreak_fit_1)

ggarrange(
  constant_plot,
  piecewise_plot,
  outbreak_plot,
  ncol = 3,
  labels = c("Constant", "Piecewise", "Outbreak"))









RSero makes it easy to compare these with the compute_information_criteria function. We will use leave-one-out cross validation to compare them (PSIS-LOO). This aims to answer the question - how well would this model predict an individual participant’s serostatus if we left them out of the fit? The resulting score is called the elpd (higher = better predictions). Below, we’ll use loo_compare() from the loo package in R to rank all of our models and give the difference in elpd from the best one


Code
constant_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(constant_fit_1)
piecewise_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(piecewise_fit_1)
outbreak_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(outbreak_fit_1)

loo::loo_compare(constant_ic_1$PSIS_LOO, piecewise_ic_1$PSIS_LOO, outbreak_ic_1$PSIS_LOO)


  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse       diag_diff diag_elpd
 model1       0.0     0.0      NA                          
 model2      -0.4     0.5    0.80 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 model3    -133.1    14.0    1.00                          


From this we can tell that model 3 (outbreak model) is clearly the worst at explaining the data. However, models 1 and 2 seem very similar and there’s a very small difference in elpd between them. Let’s take a look at the estimated FOI for both.


Code
constant_foi <- plot(constant_fit_1, YLIM = 0.3)
piecewise_foi <- plot(piecewise_fit_1, YLIM = 0.3)

# Note we need the [[1]] here as RSero's plot function returns a list where the first element is the plot we need
ggarrange(constant_foi[[1]],
          piecewise_foi[[1]],
          ncol = 2,
          labels = c("Constant", "Piecewise"))









From these plots it’s clear the piecewise model is estimating very similar FOI for the two time periods - in fact it looks almost identical to the constant model.
We can also look at the estimated parameters for the piecewise model to see when the model thinks the FOI changes to a second level


Code
parameters_credible_intervals(piecewise_fit_1)


                                        2.5%          50%       97.5%
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_1    0.3048975    0.9205434    5.206591
Year_ 2                         1994.6832418 2024.6552231 2033.675972
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_2    4.1093153    4.7383098    5.286783
                                       mean
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_1    1.920750
Year_ 2                         2021.851622
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_2    4.738982


You can see here that this estimate is really uncertain, with a 95% credible interval ranging from 1980 to 2026.
To decide between these two models we’ll follow the principle of parsimony. That is, if two models perform equally well we should choose the simplest one as it’s clear the added complexity is not needed.



In the next section you can follow the same analysis plan looking into data_2. How would you describe historical transmission of the pathogen in this dataset?






TipHint





Remember to have a look at what seroprevalence looks like by age, this will give you clues as to what models you might like to test.









Tip





We set K=1 when using piecewise and outbreak models in the first part but you can change K to look at multiple change points in FOI or multiple outbreaks in the past.







RSero paper
Salje et al 2016 - reconstructing historical CHIKV transmission in the Philippines
Hens et al 2009 - a nice review of serocatalytic models

agg_data_1 <- data_1 |> 
  mutate(age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(seq(0, 70, by = 10), Inf),
      labels = c(
        "0-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30-39",
        "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70+"),
      right = FALSE)) |> 
  group_by(age_group)  |> 
  summarise(n = n(),
            seropositive = sum(serostatus),
            seroprevalence = mean(serostatus),
            seroprevalence = seropositive / n,
            ci_lower = binom.test(seropositive, n)$conf.int[1],
            ci_upper = binom.test(seropositive, n)$conf.int[2], .groups = "drop")

ggplot(agg_data_1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = age_group, y = seroprevalence)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = age_group, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "Seroprevalence")

title: Session 2: Serocatalytic Models
text:
Next, we will prepare the data for use with RSero. RSero needs data to be in SeroData format, which needs the participants’ age at the time of sampling (age_at_sampling) and serostatus (Y).


Code
sero_data1 <- SeroData(age_at_sampling = data_1$age, Y = data_1$serostatus, sampling_year = 2024)
sero_data2 <- SeroData(age_at_sampling = data_2$age, Y = data_2$serostatus, sampling_year = 2024)


We will now define some serocatalytic models to test.
In RSero you can specify several different models of force-of-infection over time. We will look at the following.
- Constant. This is the simplest (classic) serocatalytic model which assumes a constant force of infection over time. This works well for endemic pathogens that circulate continuously in the population and are fully immunising. - Piecewise-constant. This is an extension of the classic model where we assume there have been several periods of constant force of infection. This would work well (for example) if an intervention had recently been introduced which lowered the force of infection at a particular point in time. - Outbreak. This model describes pathogen with epidemic dynamics where there have been K epidemics in the past. The model will estimate the force of infection and the timing of K previous outbreaks, assuming that FOI can be described by K Gaussian-shaped curves.


Code
constant_model <- FOImodel(type = "constant")
piecewise_model <- FOImodel(type = "piecewise", K = 2) # assuming there have been 2 phases with distinct force of infection
outbreak_model <- FOImodel(type = "outbreak", K = 1) # assuming there has been 1 outbreak in the past


Now let’s fit each model - this may take a few minutes.
You should see output from Stan on your console showing you how the sampling is progressing for each model and potentially giving you some warnings about the fit.


Code
constant_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = constant_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)
piecewise_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = piecewise_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)
outbreak_fit_1 <- fit(data = sero_data1, model = outbreak_model, iter = 1000, chains = 2)

title: Session 2: Serocatalytic Models
text:
We now have three different model fits, with very different underlying assumptions about historical transmission. First let’s compare how well each of them fit the data visually. We can do this using the RSero function seroprevalence.fit().


Code
constant_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(constant_fit_1)
piecewise_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(piecewise_fit_1)
outbreak_plot <- seroprevalence.fit(outbreak_fit_1)

ggarrange(
  constant_plot,
  piecewise_plot,
  outbreak_plot,
  ncol = 3,
  labels = c("Constant", "Piecewise", "Outbreak"))









RSero makes it easy to compare these with the compute_information_criteria function. We will use leave-one-out cross validation to compare them (PSIS-LOO). This aims to answer the question - how well would this model predict an individual participant’s serostatus if we left them out of the fit? The resulting score is called the elpd (higher = better predictions). Below, we’ll use loo_compare() from the loo package in R to rank all of our models and give the difference in elpd from the best one


Code
constant_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(constant_fit_1)
piecewise_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(piecewise_fit_1)
outbreak_ic_1 <- compute_information_criteria(outbreak_fit_1)

loo::loo_compare(constant_ic_1$PSIS_LOO, piecewise_ic_1$PSIS_LOO, outbreak_ic_1$PSIS_LOO)


  model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse       diag_diff diag_elpd
 model1       0.0     0.0      NA                          
 model2      -0.4     0.5    0.80 |elpd_diff| < 4          
 model3    -133.1    14.0    1.00                          


From this we can tell that model 3 (outbreak model) is clearly the worst at explaining the data. However, models 1 and 2 seem very similar and there’s a very small difference in elpd between them. Let’s take a look at the estimated FOI for both.


Code
constant_foi <- plot(constant_fit_1, YLIM = 0.3)
piecewise_foi <- plot(piecewise_fit_1, YLIM = 0.3)

# Note we need the [[1]] here as RSero's plot function returns a list where the first element is the plot we need
ggarrange(constant_foi[[1]],
          piecewise_foi[[1]],
          ncol = 2,
          labels = c("Constant", "Piecewise"))









From these plots it’s clear the piecewise model is estimating very similar FOI for the two time periods - in fact it looks almost identical to the constant model.
We can also look at the estimated parameters for the piecewise model to see when the model thinks the FOI changes to a second level


Code
parameters_credible_intervals(piecewise_fit_1)


                                        2.5%          50%       97.5%
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_1    0.3048975    0.9205434    5.206591
Year_ 2                         1994.6832418 2024.6552231 2033.675972
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_2    4.1093153    4.7383098    5.286783
                                       mean
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_1    1.920750
Year_ 2                         2021.851622
Annual Prob. Infection (in %)_2    4.738982


You can see here that this estimate is really uncertain, with a 95% credible interval ranging from 1980 to 2026.
To decide between these two models we’ll follow the principle of parsimony. That is, if two models perform equally well we should choose the simplest one as it’s clear the added complexity is not needed.

text:
In the next section you can follow the same analysis plan looking into data_2. How would you describe historical transmission of the pathogen in this dataset?






TipHint





Remember to have a look at what seroprevalence looks like by age, this will give you clues as to what models you might like to test.









Tip





We set K=1 when using piecewise and outbreak models in the first part but you can change K to look at multiple change points in FOI or multiple outbreaks in the past.

title: Session 1: Analysing serological data
text:
In this practical, we are going to explore the concept of the force of infection and how it relates to seroprevalence.
Download the example cross-sectional serological dataset we will be working with here: SeroStudy.csv


The aims of this practical are to:

Load and analyse a serological dataset in R
Understand how changing the force of infection affects seroprevalence by age




First, we will load in the R packages and data that we need. Take a quick look at the serosurvey dataset we are using. Note when loading this in on the R instance you will want to use this file path: read.csv("./SeroStudy.csv").


Code
library(tidyverse)




Code
sero_survey <- read.csv("../data/SeroStudy.csv")
head(sero_survey) # look at the first few rows of the dataset



What is the range and mean age of participants?







TipHint





Use range() or min() and max()





Code
sero_survey |>
  summarise(
    min_age = min(Age),
    max_age = max(Age),
    mean_age = mean(Age))



What proportion of male participants are seropositive?







TipHint





You can use table()





Code
sero_survey |>
  filter(Sex == "Male") |>
  summarise(seropos = sum(IgG == TRUE), n = n(), prop_seropositive = seropos/n)



What proportion of female participants are seropositive?



Code
sero_survey |>
  filter(Sex == "Female") |>
  summarise(seropos = sum(IgG == TRUE), n = n(), prop_seropositive = seropos/n)



Calculate the proportion seropositive by single age







TipHint





You can use a for loop or group_by and summarise





Code
prop_by_age <- sero_survey |>
  group_by(Age) |>
  summarise(seropos = sum(IgG == TRUE), n = n(), prop_seropositive = seropos/n)

prop_by_age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = prop_seropositive)) +
  geom_point()



Using the following relationship, plot the expected proportion seropositive if there was a force of infection of 0.05 in a community:

\[ P(seropositive) = 1 - e^{(-\lambda \cdot age)}\]






TipHint





Create an object lambda = 0.05 and use a vector of ages between 1 and 15 ages <- 1:15





Code
lambda <- 0.05
ages <- 1:15

expected_seropos <- data.frame(
  Age = ages,
  prop_seropositive = 1 - exp(-lambda * ages))

expected_seropos |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = prop_seropositive)) +
  geom_line()



Plot the line from no. 5 on top of the observed proportion seropositive by age – how similar does it look?



Code
prop_by_age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = prop_seropositive)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = expected_seropos, colour = "red")



Try a few different values for lambda and find one that works well



Code
lambdas <- seq(0.01, 0.15, by = 0.01)

expected_seropos_multi <- data.frame()
for (lambda in lambdas) {
  expected_seropos_multi <- rbind(
    expected_seropos_multi,
    data.frame(
      lambda = lambda,
      Age = ages,
      prop_seropositive = 1 - exp(-lambda * ages)))
}

prop_by_age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Age, y = prop_seropositive)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(
    data = expected_seropos_multi,
    aes(group = lambda),
    colour = "red", alpha = 0.4)






Using this value of lambda calculate the proportion of 30 year olds you would expect to be seropositive



Code
lambda <- 0.05 # replace with the value of lambda you found above

data.frame(Age = 30) |>
  mutate(prop_seropositive = 1 - exp(-lambda * Age))



Using this value of lambda, calculate the probability of being infected for each age between 1 and 60



Code
ages_60 <- 1:60

prob_infected <- data.frame(
  Age = ages_60,
  prob_infection = 1 - exp(-lambda * ages_60)
)

prob_infected



Assuming that there are 10,000 of each age between 1 and 60 (and no one older) – so 10,000 1 year olds, 10,000 2 year olds etc, calculate who many infections you see in total across all age groups in this population



Code
pop_uniform <- prob_infected |>
  mutate(n_people = 10000,
         n_infected = n_people * prob_infection)

pop_uniform |>
  summarise(total_infected = sum(n_infected))



Repeat the last question but assume this time there are 20,000 in each age between 1 and 10, 10,000 between 11-50 and no one older (ie a younger population of the same total size)



Code
pop_young <- prob_infected |>
  mutate(
    n_people = case_when(
      Age <= 10 ~ 20000,
      Age <= 50 ~ 10000,
      TRUE ~ 0),
    n_infected = n_people * prob_infection)

pop_young |>
  summarise(total_infected = sum(n_infected))

title: Serological modelling workshop
text:
Welcome to the workshop practicals.
The aim of this course is to understand and apply key concepts in mathematical modelling of serological data. This course is intended for public health professionals or mathematicians/statisticians with an interest in infectious disease modelling.
Throughout the course we will be using the R programming language. During the practicals we recommend:

Typing out the code (rather than copying and pasting it) as this is slower and helps you to learn
Avoiding asking large language models to write code for you during the course - while this can be useful in understanding errors in your code (if you take time to read through the response) this will not help you learn and understand.





PDU logo
